query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Spark plasma sintering at 1500 °C optimizes the binder fluidity and pore filling in a 30%-AlFeNiCoCr reinforced ZrB2 matrix, thereby enhancing the resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion compared to sintering at lower (1300 °C, 1400 °C) or higher (1600 °C) temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixed powder consisting of >99.8% pure ZrB2 (1–5 μm) and 30 wt% high-entropy-alloy binder (equimolar Al, Fe, Ni, Co, Cr) prepared by ball milling, ethanol milling, and vacuum drying.
generation.intervention: Consolidate the mixed powder using spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1500 °C under vacuum at 50 MPa with a heating rate of approximately 200 °C/min and a 5-minute hold.
generation.conditions: SPS is carried out under vacuum with a 50 MPa pressure and 200 °C/min heating rate with a 5-min dwell; corrosion tests are conducted by immersing samples in molten aluminum at 700 °C for 4, 8, or 12 days, and wear tests use a ball-on-disc setup with a Si3N4 ball at room temperature under a 10 N load, 500 r/min for 30 minutes.
generation.structural_mediator: At 1500 °C, the high-entropy alloy binder becomes sufficiently liquid to uniformly fill pores and promote strong bonding between ZrB2 grains, achieving a compact microstructure with high relative density (~97.71%).
generation.mechanism: Improved binder fluidity at 1500 °C leads to enhanced pore filling and grain bonding, which reduces the penetration pathways for molten aluminum, minimizes detachment of ZrB2 grains, and in turn lowers corrosion and wear while enhancing hardness and fracture toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The material sintered at 1500 °C is predicted to have higher relative density, greater hardness, and fracture toughness, along with a lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate and reduced wear volume, compared to cermets sintered at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, or 1600 °C and relative to pure ZrB2 ceramics.
generation.baseline: Performance is compared against ZrB2-AlFeNiCoCr cermets sintered at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, and 1600 °C, with fracture toughness of pure ZrB2 (approximately 4.5 MPa·m^1/2) serving as an additional reference.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for the specific 30%-binder composition under the given SPS parameters; variations in composition, binder percentage, sintering schedule, or test conditions (e.g., molten Al exposure at 700 °C for up to 12 days, room temperature wear tests) may not yield the same benefits.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise threshold at which binder loss occurs (observed at 1600 °C) and how minor compositional differences might affect the sintering dynamics and resultant microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of ZrB2-AlFeNiCoCr cermets by SPS at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, 1500 °C, and 1600 °C using identical pre-processing steps. Characterize microstructures with SEM/EDS and phase compositions with XRD. Measure relative density (via Archimedes method), hardness (Vickers), fracture toughness (indentation method), corrosion thickness loss after molten-aluminum exposure (at 700 °C for varied durations), and wear performance (ball-on-disc tests with a Si3N4 ball at 10 N load, 500 r/min for 30 min).
measurements: SEM/EDS imaging and XRD phase analysis
Vickers hardness and indentation fracture toughness
Molten-aluminum corrosion rate (thickness-loss) after exposures at 700 °C
Wear volume and friction coefficient from ball-on-disc tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples sintered at 1500 °C do not exhibit significantly higher density, hardness, fracture toughness, and substantially lower corrosion rate and wear volume relative to samples sintered at 1300 °C, 1400 °C, and 1600 °C, then the hypothesis is rejected.
